title: Question 4
stem:
A rigid plank is used to make a ramp between two different horizontal levels of ground, as shown in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)

Point $A$ at one end of the plank rests on the lower level of the ground. A force acts on, and is perpendicular to, the plank at point $B$. The plank is held in equilibrium by a rope that connects point $D$ on the plank to the ground. The plank has a weight that may be considered to act from its centre of gravity $C$.

The rope is perpendicular to the plank and has tension $T$. The plank is at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical.

The forces and the distances along the plank of points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are shown in Fig. 4.1.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the component of the weight that is perpendicular to the plank is $59\text{ N}$.
hints: Hint 1: Sketch the vertical 96 N arrow at C and the plank direction. The angle between them is 38 degrees, so think which side of that small right-angled triangle lies at 90 degrees to the plank.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See The Triangle Made By The Weight**
You have a vertical weight of $96\text{ N}$ acting down at C. The plank itself is tilted $38^{\circ}$ from the vertical. That means the angle between the weight vector and the line of the plank is also $38^{\circ}$.

Step 2: **Pick Out The Perpendicular Side**
If you resolve the weight into components parallel and perpendicular to the plank, the perpendicular component is opposite the $38^{\circ}$ angle. So you use sine:
$$W_{\perp} = 96 \sin 38^{\circ}$$
$$W_{\perp} \approx 59\text{ N}$$

key_concepts: resolution of a force into perpendicular components

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: By taking moments about end $A$ of the plank, calculate the tension $T$.
hints: Hint 1: Taking moments about A is clever because any force at A has zero moment. List which three forces have a moment about A and which way each one tries to turn the plank.
Hint 2: Work out each perpendicular distance from A along the plank using the 1.10 m, 0.30 m and 1.50 m lengths. Remember to use the 59 N perpendicular component for the weight, not the full 96 N.
Hint 3: Set the sum of clockwise moments equal to the sum of anticlockwise moments about A, then rearrange to isolate $T$ before putting numbers in.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose Moments About A**
In equilibrium the resultant moment is zero, so clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments. About A the force at A itself does not turn the plank, so you only need the $45\text{ N}$ force, the tension $T$ and the $59\text{ N}$ perpendicular component of weight. All three act at $90^{\circ}$ to the plank, so moment is simply force times distance along the plank from A.

Step 2: **Find Each Distance From A**
Add the sections along the plank:
$$BA = 1.10 + 0.30 + 1.50 = 2.90\text{ m}$$
$$DA = 0.30 + 1.50 = 1.80\text{ m}$$
$$CA = 1.50\text{ m}$$
The $45\text{ N}$ force tries to turn the plank one way, while $T$ and the weight component try to turn it the opposite way.

Step 3: **Balance The Moments And Solve For T**
Take anticlockwise = clockwise:
$$45 \times 2.90 = T \times 1.80 + 59 \times 1.50$$
$$130.5 = 1.80T + 88.5$$
$$1.80T = 42.0$$
$$T \approx 23\text{ N}$$
